Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) and ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) both reported recently and made the same pitch: agentic AI will power their next phase of growth. Investors have pushed back since. ServiceNow fell 27.58% over the past week, and Salesforce slipped 6.17%. The businesses below look stronger than either move suggests.

24/7 Wall St.
Agentforce Lifts Salesforce While One Guide Spooks ServiceNow Holders

Salesforce posted Q2 revenue of $11.345B, up 10.8%. That pace is steady but modest. The AI layer is growing much faster. Combined Agentforce and Data 360 ARR reached nearly $3.9B, up over 210%, and 50% of Agentforce bookings came from customers buying more credits. That tells me customers keep using agents after they go live. Marc Benioff said "We're seeing incredible demand for our AI and data products, with ARR about to cross $4 billion."

ServiceNow grew subscription revenue 21% to $3.988B, which is faster than Salesforce. It also raised its 2026 AI net new ACV target for the second time this year, to $1.7B. Still, non-GAAP EPS of $1.00 came in below the $1.02 estimate, and the Q4 cRPO guide slowed to 18.5%. Management blamed early renewals and public-sector deals that run on customers' own servers. That explanation sounds reasonable, but I want to see it confirmed.

title: Wall Street Analysts Believe Salesforce (CRM) Could Rally 26.34%: Here's is How to Trade
detail:
Wall Street Analysts Believe Salesforce (CRM) Could Rally 26.34%: Here's is How to Trade
Zacks Equity Research
Thu, November 5, 2026 at 5:55 AM PST 4 min read
CRM
Trade CRM on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Salesforce (CRM) closed the last trading session at $227.11, gaining 1.1% over the past four weeks, but there could be plenty of upside left in the stock if short-term price targets set by Wall Street analysts are any guide. The mean price target of $286.94 indicates a 26.3% upside potential.

The mean estimate comprises 50 short-term price targets with a standard deviation of $46.37. While the lowest estimate of $165.00 indicates a 27.4% decline from the current price level, the most optimistic analyst expects the stock to surge 109.2% to reach $475.00. It's very important to note the standard deviation here, as it helps understand the variability of the estimates. The smaller the standard deviation, the greater the agreement among analysts.

While the consensus price target is highly sought after by investors, the ability and unbiasedness of analysts in setting price targets have long been questionable. And investors making investment decisions solely based on this tool would arguably do themselves a disservice.

But, for CRM, an impressive average price target is not the only indicator of a potential upside. Strong agreement among analysts about the company's ability to report better earnings than they predicted earlier strengthens this view. While a positive trend in earnings estimate revisions doesn't gauge how much a stock could gain, it has proven to be powerful in predicting an upside.

Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise
Zacks Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise Chart for CRM
Here's What You Should Know About Analysts' Price Targets

According to researchers at several universities across the globe, a price target is one of many pieces of information about a stock that misleads investors far more often than it guides. In fact, empirical research shows that price targets set by several analysts, irrespective of the extent of agreement, rarely indicate where the price of a stock could actually be heading.

While Wall Street analysts have deep knowledge of a company's fundamentals and the sensitivity of its business to economic and industry issues, many of them tend to set overly optimistic price targets. Are you wondering why?

They usually do that to drum up interest in shares of companies that their firms either have existing business relationships with or are looking to be associated with. In other words, business incentives of firms covering a stock often result in inflated price targets set by analysts.

However, a tight clustering of price targets, which is represented by a low standard deviation, indicates that analysts have a high degree of agreement about the direction and magnitude of a stock's price movement. While that doesn't necessarily mean the stock will hit the average price target, it could be a good starting point for further research aimed at identifying the potential fundamental driving forces.

Twilio Inc. TWLO shares have come under pressure since the company reported its third-quarter 2026 results on Oct. 29. The stock has plunged 11.7% since then, as investors reacted negatively to management's fourth-quarter guidance, which points to slower organic revenue growth and lower adjusted earnings than the third quarter.

For the fourth quarter, Twilio expects reported and organic revenue growth in the range of 17%-17.5% and 11%-12%, respectively, year over year. Non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) are expected to be between $1.48 and $1.53, signifying a year-over-year growth of 11%-15%. Fourth-quarter projections for these metrics indicate a slower growth rate than in the third quarter.

While slowdown concerns are understandable, the sell-off appears to overlook Twilio's improving profitability, strong cash flow generation and growing opportunities in artificial intelligence (AI). The company continues to benefit from healthy demand for its communications platform and software add-ons. Given its improving financial performance and promising AI prospects, the recent decline could offer investors an attractive entry point.

TWLO's Q3 Performance Shows Broad-Based Business Strength

Twilio delivered a strong third-quarter performance, with revenues growing 20% year over year to $1.56 billion. Organic revenue growth, excluding incremental U.S. carrier pass-through fees and acquisition-related revenues, was 16%.

Growth was broad-based across its business. Messaging revenues increased 24% year over year, supported by higher volumes and growing adoption of WhatsApp and Rich Communication Services. Voice revenues advanced more than 20%, driven by volume growth and increased adoption of software add-ons. Revenues from software add-ons grew more than 25% year over year, while support and services revenues increased 30%.

Twilio's self-serve channel delivered more than 30% revenue growth, while revenues from independent software vendors rose more than 20%. Customer expansion also remained encouraging. Its dollar-based net expansion rate was 114%, up from 109% in the prior-year quarter. This indicates that existing customers are spending more on Twilio's platform as their communication requirements expand.

Profitability was another major highlight. Non-GAAP gross profit increased 18% year over year to $768 million. Non-GAAP income from operations surged 39% to $326 million, while its operating margin improved 290 basis points to 21%. Non-GAAP EPS jumped 32% to $1.65.

Strategy Inc. (MSTR), formerly known as MicroStrategy, sells software and holds Bitcoin. The company spent more cash than it brought in during each of the last four quarters. That gap was $584 million in the quarter ended September 30, 2026. So take a guess: if it kept burning cash at that pace and raised nothing, how many quarters would the money it holds cover?

How Fast Is Strategy Burning Cash?

In the quarter ended September 30, 2026, Strategy burned cash equal to 465.7% of its sales, down from 3,861% in the same quarter a year earlier. Burn here means free cash flow below zero: the cash left after running the business and paying for capital spending.

Because the day-to-day business brought in slightly more cash than it used, all of the latest burn came from capital spending. The cash burn over the last four quarters was less than half that of the four quarters before. Still, the burn has not stopped in any of the last eight quarters.

How Long Would Strategy's Cash Last?

Strategy held $5.9 billion in cash and short-term investments on September 30, 2026. If the company kept burning cash at the average pace of the last four quarters and raised nothing, those reserves would cover about a quarter and a half. Most of that outflow was Bitcoin buying, which Strategy has paid for by raising new money.

The cash lasts under a year unless the burn stays at its latest, slower pace. At $6.78 billion, Strategy's debt is also larger than that cash balance.

Who Has Paid For The Burn So Far?

Existing shareholders have paid for much of the burn. Strategy's share count rose 117% in the two years to September 30, 2026: the company sold new shares, leaving each existing share with a smaller piece of the company. Debt grew about 59% over the same two years, though it is lower than a year ago.

Management said on the October 29 call that Strategy raised about $5.4 billion in the September quarter alone, and $21.2 billion so far in 2026. The company has paid for its spending with this new money rather than with cash it already had.

title: What Is Going On With Zoom Stock?

What Is Going On With Zoom Stock?

Zoom Communications (ZM) stock trades at 8.3 times earnings, compared with a 22.8 multiple for the median S&P 500 company, though on operating profit its $26.9 billion market value is about 23 times. Yet the software maker expanded its sales, margins and cash flow over the twelve months to July 2026. Zoom shares returned 5.4% in the year to November 2, 2026, trailing the 10.3% rise in the S&P 500 index. Either a sound business is on sale, or the low price is a fair one. So what are you actually buying at $91.98 a share?

Zoom Is Growing And Holds $7.25 Billion In Cash

You are buying a profitable software business holding far more cash than debt. At the end of July 2026, Zoom had $7.25 billion in cash and short-term investments against about $60 million of debt. Spread across 300 million diluted shares, that cash equals about $24 a share. The company's products include Zoom Workplace, Zoom Phone and Zoom Contact Center.

The business also earns well. Over the twelve months to July 2026, Zoom recorded an operating margin of 23.7%, compared with 18.6% for the median S&P 500 company. The company carries a 7.1% free cash flow yield, measuring free cash flow against market value. Management is returning cash to shareholders through buybacks, repurchasing about $352 million of stock in fiscal Q2 2027. Based on those figures, the low multiple looks like a discount on a sound business.

Zoom's Net Income Is Nearly Triple Its Operating Profit

That 8.3 multiple is based on $3.26 billion in net income over the twelve months to July 2026, a figure almost three times the $1.19 billion Zoom earned from its operations. This gap is widest in fiscal Q2 2027, when net income was $1.54 billion against operating income of $314 million. Zoom's non-GAAP results, which exclude net gains on strategic investments, came to $1.55 a share in that quarter.

The multiple fell alongside that jump in profit, rather than falling with the share price. When measuring the end-of-June share price against profit for the twelve months to July, Zoom traded at 19.8 times earnings in 2025 and 7.8 times in 2026. Over the same year, its price to sales barely moved, inching from 5.0 to 5.1.

Beneath that profit, the business is growing slowly. Revenue expanded 2.8% in the twelve months to July 2024 and 3.6% a year later. While the growth rate reached 5.0% in the latest twelve months, it remains below the 8.5% for the median S&P 500 company. Management also expects its online business to remain flat in fiscal 2027.

title: S&P cuts Salesforce to ’A’ on rising acquisition debt and buybacks

S&P cuts Salesforce to ’A’ on rising acquisition debt and buybacks

Investing.com -- S&P Global Ratings downgraded Salesforce Inc (NYSE:CRM) to 'A' from 'A+', pointing to an increasingly aggressive capital allocation strategy characterized by debt-funded shareholder returns and large-scale acquisitions. The ratings agency highlighted that recent dealmaking, alongside a $25 billion debt-financed share repurchase program, has pushed pro forma net debt-to-EBITDA above its previous 2x downgrade threshold.

The rating action reflects mounting risks that leverage could climb further as the enterprise software maker pursues an ambitious long-term expansion blueprint. S&P expects management will prioritize growth investments and buybacks over balance-sheet cash accumulation to reach its goal of expanding revenue from approximately $44 billion today to more than $63 billion by 2030.

That expansion push has already catalyzed significant deal activity, including pending or completed takeovers of Informatica for $9.5 billion, Braze for $5.7 billion, and Fin for $3.6 billion. S&P noted that Salesforce's organic revenue momentum has moderated, leaving the company increasingly reliant on programmatic M&A to generate 3 to 4 percentage points of its projected 11% fiscal 2027 top-line growth.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

Near-term execution across core subscription operations remains solid, anchored by a 14% year-over-year lift in remaining performance obligations during the second quarter. While growth across the company's marketing and commerce offerings has softened recently, S&P indicated the Braze transaction could help reverse that trend and reinforce cross-selling momentum.

Longer term, Salesforce is directing resources toward monetizing its Data360 and Agentforce frameworks, which generated $3.9 billion in annual recurring revenue in the second quarter. Strong adoption of agentic AI offerings could lift customer spending by 1.5x to 2.0x and mitigate seat attrition risks, though the agency cautioned that material top-line contributions are unlikely over the next two fiscal years.

S&P assigned a stable outlook to the revised rating, projecting that strong free operating cash flow will allow Salesforce to sustain net leverage below 2.5x while defending its enterprise footprint. The agency warned, however, that further debt-funded buybacks, larger transactions pushing leverage beyond 2.5x, or disruptive AI competition could trigger additional downward rating pressure.

title: Salesforce Stock Has Only Done This Twice Before. Here's What History Suggests Happens Next.
detail:
Salesforce Stock Has Only Done This Twice Before. Here's What History Suggests Happens Next.
Jake Lerch, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 4, 2026 at 10:50 AM PST 5 min read
CRM
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

What's your first thought when you see "half off" at the bakery? Are you eager to snap up a quick deal, or do you assume the bread's gone stale? A similar question emerges in the stock market.

Take Salesforce (NYSE: CRM), for example. The company's stock has endured a rough patch over the last two years. At its June 2026 low, the stock had dropped more than 59% from its all-time high.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But to decide whether Salesforce is a ready-made bargain or a week-old baguette, we need to examine the details.

Image source: Getty Images.
Salesforce's 50% stock declines are rare

Salesforce has been a public company since 2004. In its more than 22 years as a public company, its stock has dropped 50% or more from its all-time high on only three occasions:

CRM data by YCharts

Oct. 7, 2008: Salesforce stock fell sharply, along with the broader market, as the financial crisis shook Wall Street. Salesforce stock ultimately declined by 70% before bottoming in November 2008.

Sept. 1, 2022: Salesforce stock melted slowly throughout late 2021 and nearly all of 2022 during the latest bear market. After crossing the 50% threshold in September 2022, the stock bottomed in December 2022, down 59% from its all-time high, before recovering and setting new all-time highs in 2024.

Feb. 23, 2026: Salesforce stock fell below the 50% mark in February 2026 as market participants fretted over whether software-as-a-service (SaaS) business models would withstand rapid innovations in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector.

These drops aren't garden-variety pullbacks; they are rare structural resets. And in the latest case, a recovery may already be underway.

Past recoveries rewarded patience, not perfect timing

So, let's see what happened in the past. In each case, we'll assume an investor bought the day after the 50% level was crossed. In the 2008 case, shares gained 63% in the year after the breach. In 2022, Salesforce stock rose 44% in the following 12 months. However, there's one very important caveat: Things got worse before they got better. In 2008, shares dropped another 39% before the bottom was truly in. In 2022, shares fell another 16%.

In other words, while a 50% drop is massive for Salesforce stock, investors shouldn't think of it as a line in the sand. The stock can -- and has -- fallen even further before. Past rebounds show resilience, but today's recovery requires a clear-eyed look at the current business.
